# Correspondence transport recipe (v1)

Schema for `.tera/correspondence-transports/<name>.hcl` recipes per [ADR-119](../adr/ADR-119-the-correspondence-transport-port.md) D1. A **correspondence transport** is a **carrier class** — Telegram-the-carrier-class, the-workbench-inbox-the-carrier-class — and this recipe is where it declares what a carrier of that class can actually do. Transports differ in ways that are not hideable: Telegram has reply-to-message-id, Slack has `thread_ts`, email has `In-Reply-To` and SMS has nothing at all; Telegram and Slack can withdraw a delivered message and SMS cannot; WhatsApp's Business API cannot send arbitrary outbound outside a 24-hour window without a pre-approved template. So the descriptor states five facets — correlation, interaction (`native_contracts`), mutability, initiation and attachment carriage — and the spine assumes none of them.

**A capability is declared, never probed and never assumed.** Every facet is required and none has a default. A probe is unreliable, per-account and fails in the dangerous direction — one that times out reads as *cannot* and one that succeeds once is cached into an assumption — so declared beats discovered, and an undeclared facet is refused offline by `tera validate` rather than guessed at. There is deliberately no conservative default either: an absent declaration is the case where nobody has decided, and deciding it silently is a permissive default wearing a conservative hat, which [ADR-075](../adr/ADR-075-per-principal-resource-governance.md) D11 refuses by ruling.

**It names a class, never a party and never a credential.** There is no field here for a person, a chat id, an account or an endpoint: [ADR-118](../adr/ADR-118-enrollment-and-correspondence-authorization.md) D1 rules that correspondence introduces no addressing namespace — the authenticated principal is the address and there is no second registry — so there is no party recipe kind and no directory of people in HCL. And there is no field for a bot token, an API key or a password, because a credential in a vault file is a credential in a git tree; the block admits no unmodelled attribute either, so neither can arrive as one nobody described.

**A declaration resolves, and it is still only a label.** This kind is read on the enrollment path: the correspondence service resolves an enrollment binding's transport class through the domain's own `correspondence.TransportDeclarations` port, refuses a class no recipe declares, and hands the resolved descriptor's five facets to the spine — which reads them to correlate a reply, degrade a response contract before a carrier ever sees it, settle a delivered question, decide whether an endpoint may be sent to unprompted, and resolve an attachment. Carriers deliver against those facets: `workbench-inbox` is the reference carrier the spine ships with, and `telegram` is the first external one, enrolled through a verifier of its own. Resolution is live, so declaring a class makes the next enrollment against it resolve and removing one makes the next enrollment refuse, without a restart in either direction. What none of that establishes is who is on the other end: a transport class recorded against an enrolled window is a label saying which carrier the window is on, and a label is never evidence that anybody controls a transport identity — that is a verification handshake's job.

The file stem is the carrier class name, so `telegram.hcl` declares the class `telegram`. The recipe declares a single `correspondence_transport` block whose label must equal that stem.

## Example

A minimal `correspondence-transport`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/correspondence-transports/example-correspondence-transport.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

correspondence_transport "example-correspondence-transport" {
  description         = "The workbench inbox: the reference carrier, for a browser window over its own authenticated session. The server side stays wired; no client in this repository opens such a window today."
  correlation         = "native-thread"
  native_contracts    = ["text"]
  mutability          = "edit"
  initiation          = "unrestricted"
  attachment_carriage = "bytes"
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | string | yes | — | — | const `v1` | Per-recipe grammar version. Required; this schema applies when version is v1. |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | min length 1 | Bare carrier-class name (the HCL block label), which must equal the filename stem. It names a CLASS OF CARRIER and not a party: telegram.hcl declares the class telegram, and workbench-inbox.hcl declares the reference carrier the spine ships with. The loader namespaces the recipe as <vault-id>/correspondence-transports/<name>. IT IS NOT A PERSON, AN ENDPOINT, AN ACCOUNT OR A CONNECTOR INSTANCE - ADR-118 D1 rules that correspondence introduces no addressing namespace at all, because the authenticated principal IS the address and a second registry of people is the thing that decision exists to prevent, so there is no party recipe kind and nothing in this grammar names a human being. A binding from a person to an endpoint on one of these carriers is per-principal runtime state written by a verification handshake, never operator HCL. And the class name is a LABEL rather than evidence: a window recorded as being on telegram says nothing whatever about who controls it, which is what the handshake establishes and what this declaration cannot. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Free prose saying which carrier this is and what a deployment reaches through it. Optional, and it earns its place in a grammar that is otherwise five closed vocabularies because the five say what the carrier CAN DO and none of them says what it IS - a reader looking at a descriptor of native-thread, buttons and unrestricted initiation cannot tell Slack from Telegram from a bespoke internal bus, and the difference decides whether a deployment is comfortable putting a doorbell snapshot on it. |
| `correlation` | string | yes | — | — | one of `native-thread`, `token-in-body`, `none` | ADR-119 D1 REPLY-CORRELATION facet, consumed by D3: how a reply is attributed to the message it answers. Getting yes, staging back to the right one of four outstanding questions is where this subsystem lives or dies, and the mechanism is per carrier. native-thread captures the carrier own reply reference at send and matches it on receipt - Telegram reply-to, Slack thread_ts, email In-Reply-To - and is preferred wherever it exists. token-in-body has the spine embed a short token in the rendered message and require it in the reply, for a carrier with no threading. none is SMS, and the spine constrains the CONVERSATION instead: at most one outstanding question per window at a time, so an uncorrelated reply is unambiguous by construction. THE FALLBACK IS THE SPINE DECISION AND NEVER THE ADAPTER - an adapter inventing its own correlation scheme would be a second implementation of the hardest part of this subsystem, and the failure it produces is an answer applied to the wrong question, which is silent and consequential. A carrier declaring none is a DEGRADED carrier rather than an equal one, and a deployment relying on one should know that before it depends on it. Required, and there is no default: this is the facet whose wrong guess misroutes an answer. |
| `native_contracts` | string[] | yes | — | — | min items 1; items one of `text`, `ack`, `confirm`, `choice`, `form` | ADR-119 D1 INTERACTION facet, consumed by D2: which of the closed response-contract set this carrier renders NATIVELY - buttons, quick replies - as against needing the spine to degrade it to text. The set is closed at ack, confirm, choice, text and form for a stated reason: a carrier can only map a closed set, and an open one would push the mapping decision back out to each adapter, which is the arrangement D2 exists to prevent. DEGRADATION LIVES IN THE SPINE AND HAPPENS EXACTLY ONCE, so an adapter receives something it can render and has no branch for the case it cannot: a choice becomes a numbered text prompt, a form becomes a prompt, a confirm becomes a yes/no question. TEXT IS REQUIRED IN THE LIST because text is what every other contract degrades TO - a carrier that renders no text has nothing to degrade to, so the spine would have no way to put any contract in front of a correspondent on it, and the combination is refused offline. The smallest honest declaration is a list of just text: that is the SMS-shaped carrier, on which everything degrades, and it is a complete statement rather than a gap. It is NOT the same as omitting the attribute, which is refused as an undeclared facet. A message with no response contract is the same object and the same path - a weekly report is a message a carrier renders and nobody answers - so this facet is about what a carrier can ASK, never about whether it can send. |
| `mutability` | string | yes | — | — | one of `edit`, `withdraw`, `neither` | ADR-119 D1 MUTABILITY facet, consumed by D4: which mechanism the spine uses to settle a delivered message on a window that did not answer, discharging ADR-117 D9. edit and withdraw are the two ways a carrier can act on a message it has already delivered; neither is SMS, where the message is SUPERSEDED by a follow-up saying it was settled rather than silently left standing. BOTH HALVES OF D4 ARE REQUIRED AND NEITHER SUBSTITUTES FOR THE OTHER: retraction alone fails on carriers that cannot retract, on clock skew, and on a tap already in flight, while a late-reply refusal alone leaves a live button offering an action that will be rejected, which trains people to distrust the buttons - and the buttons are the whole ergonomic argument for this subsystem. A carrier able to do BOTH declares the one this deployment wants used; under-declaring is safe in D1 stated direction, because the cost of assuming LESS is a superseded message left standing and the cost of assuming MORE is a live Unlock? button on a question that was answered forty seconds ago. Required, and there is no default. |
| `initiation` | string | yes | — | — | one of `unrestricted`, `reply-window-only` | ADR-119 D1 INITIATION facet, consumed by D6: whether this carrier can be sent to unprompted, or only inside a live window the correspondent opened. A carrier declaring reply-window-only may be selected for delivery ONLY when such a window exists; otherwise the spine treats that endpoint as it treats one below its floor - not an error, not a retry loop, just an endpoint this message does not reach - and the message is still in the inbox. THIS FACET IS IN THE FIRST RELEASE FOR A CARRIER TERA DOES NOT YET SUPPORT, WHICH IS DELIBERATE: WhatsApp Business API cannot send arbitrary outbound outside a 24-hour window without a pre-approved template, and the point of encoding the constraint now is that the alternative is discovering it after N adapters have been written against a port that cannot express it, at which point every one of them moves. The cost today is one field and one branch in selection. A DEPLOYMENT WHOSE ONLY CARRIER IS REPLY-WINDOW-ONLY HAS A CORRESPONDENCE SYSTEM THAT CANNOT PAGE ANYBODY, and tera validate says so at configuration time rather than at 02:00 - as do tera config plan and tera config apply, which is the golden path for authoring a vault recipe kind and the only path that reaches a user vault at all. Both callers share one advisory sentence and each names the scope it could actually see, because two advisories about one condition disagreeing about what they saw is the warning an operator learns to ignore. Required, and there is no default. |
| `attachment_carriage` | string | yes | — | — | one of `bytes`, `fetchable-url`, `none` | ADR-119 D1 ATTACHMENT-CARRIAGE facet, consumed by D5: what this carrier can be handed when a message carries an attachment. Attachments are ADR-107 artifacts BY REFERENCE, and the port resolves a reference into whatever this says the carrier can take - uploaded bytes for a bot API, a scoped expiring fetchable-url for a browser, and nothing for a carrier that takes neither, IN WHICH CASE THE MESSAGE IS DELIVERED WITHOUT THE ATTACHMENT RATHER THAN NOT DELIVERED. Resolution happens at DELIVERY time rather than at send time, because one message may go to windows with different carriage and different content classes: one message, several resolutions. IT IS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE CARRIER AND NOT A PERMISSION - what may actually be resolved for a given window is ADR-118 D9 content class, which composes with this and answers the other question: can it, versus may it. A doorbell snapshot reaching a public bot API is a decision somebody made rather than a default, and an expiring URL handed to a consumer cloud is an egress event even though no bytes left the deployment. Required, and there is no default. |
